tool.name: MongoDB
tool.tagline: Document database that stores flexible JSON-like records at scale
tool.description: MongoDB is a general-purpose document database: records are JSON-like BSON documents grouped in collections, queried with a rich filter language and an aggregation pipeline. It is popular for web and mobile back ends because documents map naturally to objects in code, and it scales out with replica sets and sharding.

glossary.def: In MongoDB, one record: a set of named fields and their values, shaped like a JavaScript object. It can contain nested objects and arrays.
In MongoDB, a named group of documents inside a database, roughly what a table is in SQL, but without a fixed set of columns.
A document stored as a value inside another document, such as an address object inside a customer.
Binary JSON: the format MongoDB uses to store and send documents. Same structure as JSON, but packed as bytes and with extra types such as dates, ObjectIds and exact decimals.
MongoDB's default id value: 12 bytes, shown as 24 hexadecimal characters, starting with the time it was created, so ids roughly follow creation order.
The MongoDB Shell: a program you run in a terminal to type JavaScript commands to a MongoDB server and see the results.
An address in web-address style, such as mongodb://localhost:27017, that tells a program where the MongoDB server is and how to log in.
MongoDB's own online service that runs MongoDB databases for you, so you only connect to them.
What a MongoDB query returns: an object that hands you the matching documents a batch at a time instead of loading them all at once.
The error (code 11000) MongoDB gives when a write would create a second document with the same _id or the same value in a field declared unique.
In MongoDB, the part of a query that chooses which fields of each matching document come back, like the column list in an SQL SELECT.
A special $ key used in a MongoDB filter, such as $gt (greater than) or $in (one of these values), to match more than plain equality.
A special $ key that says how to change a document, such as $set (set a field) or $inc (add to a number).
A $ placeholder in an update path, such as items.$.qty, that stands for the array element(s) to change.
A MongoDB index on a date field with an expiry time; the server automatically deletes documents once their date is older than that.
Answering a query by reading every document in the collection, because no index helps. Fine for tiny collections, slow for big ones.
An index on an array field, with one entry per array element, so queries for any element are fast.
An index on several fields at once, sorted by the first field, then by the second within it, and so on, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name.
A guideline for ordering fields in a MongoDB compound index: Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields.
A query answered entirely from an index, without reading the documents themselves, because every field it filters on and returns is in the index.
MongoDB's way of computing reports: documents pass through a list of stages, each filtering, reshaping, grouping or sorting the output of the previous one.
One step of a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, such as $match (filter) or $group (group and total).
In a MongoDB $group stage, a calculation that combines many values into one, such as $sum, $avg or $max.
One way an application reads or writes data, such as 'show an order with its items'. MongoDB schemas are designed around these.
In MongoDB, storing related data inside the parent document (an order's items inside the order) instead of in a separate collection.
In MongoDB, storing another document's _id instead of a copy of it, and looking that document up separately when needed.
The main object of a MongoDB driver: it holds the connections to the server, and you get databases and collections from it.
A group of MongoDB servers holding the same data, usually three: one primary takes the writes and the others copy them, ready to take over if it fails.
The MongoDB server program itself, the one that stores the data and answers queries.
In a MongoDB replica set, the one member that accepts writes; the others copy its changes.
In a MongoDB replica set, a member that keeps a copy of the data by replaying the primary's changes, and can become primary if it fails.
The operations log: a fixed-size collection on a MongoDB primary listing every change, which secondaries read and replay to stay in sync.
In a MongoDB replica set, the vote the members hold to choose a new primary when the current one can't be reached.
A MongoDB setting saying when a write counts as done: once the primary has it (w: 1) or once a majority of members have it (w: 'majority').
A MongoDB setting saying how safe the data a read returns must be, e.g. only data a majority of replica-set members already have.
A MongoDB setting choosing which replica-set member serves reads: the primary, a secondary, or the nearest one.
MongoDB's on-disk log of recent writes, saved before the data files are updated, so the writes can be replayed after a crash.
In MongoDB, a context the driver opens to tie several operations together, used for transactions and for reading your own writes.
A MongoDB transaction that changes several documents or collections all-or-nothing, as opposed to a single-document write, which is always atomic.
A MongoDB setup where each collection's data is split across several replica sets (shards), with mongos routers sending each query to the right ones.
The MongoDB router program in a sharded cluster: applications connect to it, and it forwards each operation to the shards that hold the data.
In a MongoDB sharded cluster, the servers that keep the map of which ranges of data live on which shard.
The MongoDB background process that moves ranges of data between shards so each holds a similar share.
A sharded query that has to ask every shard and combine their answers because it doesn't include the shard key; as slow as the slowest shard.
MongoDB's storage engine: the part that lays data out on disk, caches it in memory, compresses it and recovers it after a crash.
The documents and index entries a database touches regularly. For good speed it has to fit in memory.
Removing data from a full cache or memory to make room for new data.
In MongoDB, a moment (every 60 seconds by default) when WiredTiger writes a consistent copy of all changed data to the data files, so recovery only replays the journal from there.
One possible way of running a query, for example using one index or another. MongoDB tries several and keeps the fastest.
Where MongoDB remembers the winning plan for each query shape, so later queries of that shape skip the trial.
The structure of a MongoDB query, which fields it filters, sorts and returns, ignoring the actual values. Queries of the same shape share a cached plan.
A query suddenly switching to a different, often slower, plan, for example after its cached plan was chosen for different values.

concepts.name: Documents, collections and BSON
concepts.summary: MongoDB stores data as documents (records shaped like JavaScript objects) in collections, saved in a typed format called BSON.
concepts.why: Every other MongoDB skill starts from knowing what a document is and how it differs from a table row.
concepts.body:
Think of a paper form, like a customer sign-up card: it has named slots (name, email, phone) with a value written in each. MongoDB stores data as **documents** that work the same way. Each named slot is a **field**, and a document is a set of field/value pairs, written just like a JavaScript object: `{ name: "Ana", age: 31 }`.

A value can itself be an object (an **embedded document**, such as an address inside a customer) or an array (such as a list of tags). That lets one document hold a whole thing your app works with, like an order together with its line items, instead of spreading it over several tables.

Documents are grouped into **collections**, roughly what a table is in SQL, and collections live in databases on a MongoDB server. Unlike a table, a collection has no fixed schema by default: two documents in the same collection may have different fields.

Every document has an `_id` field that is unique within its collection, like a primary key. If you don't supply one, the **driver** (the ready-made code your program uses to talk to MongoDB) creates an **ObjectId**: a 12-byte value that starts with the time it was made, so ids roughly follow creation order.

People often call documents "JSON-like". **JSON** is a common text format for data that looks almost exactly like a JavaScript object, and it is how documents are usually shown on screen.

MongoDB doesn't store that text, though. It stores **BSON** ("binary JSON"): the same structure packed as raw bytes instead of readable characters, which is quicker to read and has more data types:

- `ObjectId` for ids, `Date` for dates and times (counted in milliseconds since 1 January 1970, UTC),
- `Int32` and `Int64` for whole numbers of two sizes, `Double` for floating-point numbers, and `Decimal128` for exact decimals (use it for money),
- `Binary`, `Boolean`, `Null`, embedded documents and arrays.

Types matter when you search: a query for `{ price: 5 }` compares type and value, so the string `"5"` does not match the number 5. Field order inside a document is kept, and one document can be at most 16 MB (megabytes: about 16 million bytes).
takeaways: Database > collection > document; documents are nested JSON-like objects
Every document has a unique _id, an ObjectId by default
BSON adds real types: Date, ObjectId, Int64, Decimal128
Documents are capped at 16 MB
pitfalls: Storing dates as strings: you lose date range queries and date operators; store real Date values.

quiz.q: Which document matches the filter { qty: 5 }?
quiz.explain: Comparisons respect BSON type, so the string "5" is not equal to the number 5.

quiz.q: What does MongoDB do if you insert a document without an _id?
options: Leaves the document without an id
quiz.explain: The driver (or server) adds an ObjectId _id automatically.

concepts.name: Connecting with mongosh
concepts.summary: Use the MongoDB Shell (mongosh) to connect to a server, switch databases and run commands written in JavaScript.
concepts.why: mongosh is the quickest way to explore data, try queries and look after a running database.
concepts.body:
To talk to a MongoDB server by hand, you type commands into a **shell**: a program in your terminal that reads a command, runs it and prints the result. MongoDB's shell is **mongosh**. It is a JavaScript REPL built on Node.js, so everything you type is JavaScript.

You start it with a **connection string**, an address that says where the server is, much like the address of a website. `mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27017"` connects to a server on your own computer (**localhost**); 27017 is the number MongoDB listens on by default.

For a database hosted on **Atlas**, MongoDB's online hosting service, the string looks like `mongosh "mongodb+srv://cluster0.example.mongodb.net/" --username ana`.

A few shell commands get you oriented:

- `show dbs` lists databases, `use shop` switches to the `shop` database,
- `show collections` lists collections in the current database,
- `db` is the current database object, and `db.orders` is the `orders` collection.

A database or collection is only created the first time you write to it, so `use typo` followed by a find just returns nothing rather than an error. Watch for spelling mistakes.

Because the shell is JavaScript, you can use variables, loops and functions: `const cutoff = new Date("2026-01-01")`, then pass `cutoff` in a query.

A query doesn't hand back all its results at once. It returns a **cursor**, an object that gives you the results a batch at a time. The shell prints the first 20 documents and you type `it` to see more. `.toArray()` collects everything into an array, which is fine for small results.

Use `db.orders.help()` or press Tab to see the available methods, and `exit` to leave. Your application code will talk to MongoDB through a driver instead of the shell, but the queries look almost the same.
concepts.code:
// $ mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27017"
show dbs                    // admin, config, local, ...
use shop                    // switched to db shop
db.orders.insertOne({ status: "new", total: 12 })
show collections            // orders  (created by the first write)
const big = db.orders.find({ total: { $gt: 10 } }).toArray()
big.length                  // 1
db.orders.countDocuments()  // 1
db.getName()                // shop
takeaways: mongosh is a JavaScript REPL: use, show dbs, show collections, db.<coll>
Databases and collections are created on first write
find returns a cursor; type it for the next batch
pitfalls: Misspelling a collection name: you silently query an empty, nonexistent collection.

quiz.q: You run use reports in mongosh but never insert anything. What happens?
options: An empty reports database is created on disk
Nothing is created until the first write
reports becomes the default database for all users
quiz.explain: Databases and collections are created lazily on the first write.

concepts.name: Inserting documents
concepts.summary: Add documents with insertOne and insertMany and understand what they return.
concepts.why: Adding data is the first step of every feature that creates, reads, updates or deletes records (CRUD).
concepts.body:
`insertOne(doc)` adds one document and returns `{ acknowledged: true, insertedId: ... }`. `insertMany([docs])` adds several in one **round trip** (one message to the server and one reply, instead of one per document) and returns all the new ids in `insertedIds`.

If the target collection doesn't exist it is created. If a document has no `_id`, one is generated. Inserting a document whose `_id` already exists fails with a **duplicate key error**, code 11000. The same happens for any other field you have declared unique (with a unique index, shown in the indexes lessons).

`insertMany` is **ordered** by default: it inserts documents in sequence and stops at the first error, leaving earlier documents inserted. Pass `{ ordered: false }` to let the server continue past failures and insert everything it can, which is also faster when loading lots of data. Either way, a multi-document insert is not a transaction: a failure part way through does not roll back what was already written.

Each single-document write is atomic: other readers see the whole document or none of it, even when it contains nested arrays and objects. That is a key reason to model related data inside one document when it is read and written together.

To load a whole file of data, MongoDB has a separate program, `mongoimport`. Inside code, `bulkWrite` sends a mix of inserts, updates and deletes in one batch.
takeaways: insertOne returns insertedId; insertMany returns insertedIds
Duplicate _id or unique key: error 11000
ordered: true (default) stops at the first error; ordered: false continues
Single-document writes are atomic; multi-document inserts are not
pitfalls: Assuming a failed insertMany inserted nothing: documents before the error (or all valid ones, if unordered) are kept.

quiz.q: An ordered insertMany of five documents hits a duplicate key on the third. How many are inserted?
quiz.explain: Ordered inserts stop at the first error, so the first two stay inserted.

concepts.name: Finding documents and projections
concepts.summary: Read documents with find and findOne, filter by field values and nested fields, and choose returned fields.
concepts.why: Almost every screen in an app is backed by a find query.
concepts.body:
`find(filter, projection)` returns a cursor over matching documents; `findOne` returns the first match or `null`. The **filter** is itself a document: `{ status: "paid" }` means status equals "paid", and several fields are combined with AND: `{ status: "paid", country: "AM" }`. An empty filter `{}` matches everything.

To reach inside embedded documents use **dot notation** with quotes: `{ "customer.email": "ana@example.com" }`. Matching a whole embedded document, `{ customer: { email: "..." } }`, instead requires an exact match of the entire embedded document, including field order, which is rarely what you want.

The **projection** (the second argument) chooses which fields come back, so less data travels over the network:

- `{ name: 1, price: 1 }` returns only those fields plus `_id`,
- `{ _id: 0, name: 1 }` also drops `_id`,
- `{ description: 0 }` returns everything except `description`.

You cannot mix inclusions and exclusions in one projection, except for excluding `_id`.

A `null` filter value matches both documents where the field is `null` and documents where it is missing. To test presence explicitly use `{ field: { $exists: true } }`, covered with the other operators next.
takeaways: Filter fields are ANDed; {} matches everything
Use "a.b" dot notation to filter on embedded fields
Projection: 1 to include, 0 to exclude, never both (except _id)
{ field: null } matches null and missing
pitfalls: Filtering with a whole embedded document { address: { city: 'X' } }, which needs an exact match of the entire object.

quiz.q: Which filter finds users whose embedded address.city is "Paris" regardless of other address fields?
quiz.explain: Dot notation matches one embedded field; the whole-object form requires an exact match of the entire address.

concepts.name: Query operators
concepts.summary: Use operators like $gt, $in, $or, $exists and $regex in filters to match ranges, alternatives, missing fields and text patterns.
concepts.why: Real queries need ranges, alternatives and missing-field checks, not just equality.
concepts.body:
Operators start with `$` and go where a value would: `{ age: { $gte: 18, $lt: 65 } }` means 18 to 64.

- **Comparison**: `$eq`, `$ne`, `$gt`, `$gte`, `$lt`, `$lte`, `$in`, `$nin`. `{ status: { $in: ["paid", "shipped"] } }` is a compact OR on one field.
- **Logical**: `$or`, `$and`, `$nor` take an array of filters; `$not` negates one operator expression. `{ $or: [{ vip: true }, { total: { $gt: 100 } }] }`.
- **Element**: `$exists: true/false` tests presence; `$type: "string"` tests the BSON type.
- **Evaluation**: `$regex` matches text against a **regular expression** (a pattern language for text, like SQL's LIKE but more powerful); `$expr` compares two fields of the same document, e.g. `{ $expr: { $gt: ["$spent", "$budget"] } }`.

You rarely need `$and` explicitly, because listing several fields already ANDs them. You do need it when combining two `$or` clauses, since a document can't have two `$or` keys.

Watch what negation means: `$ne` and `$nin` also match documents where the field is missing, and they usually can't use an index efficiently. A pattern that may match anywhere in the text, or that ignores upper and lower case, like `/smith/i`, has to check every value. Only a pattern tied to the start with `^` that respects case, such as `/^smi/`, can use an index.
takeaways: Operators go in the value position: { field: { $op: value } }
$in is OR over one field; $or combines whole sub-filters
$exists and $type test presence and BSON type; $expr compares fields
$ne/$nin also match missing fields and rarely use an index well
pitfalls: Writing { age: { $gt: 18 }, age: { $lt: 30 } }: duplicate keys in a JS object keep only the last; put both operators in one object.

quiz.q: Which filter finds orders with status "paid" or "shipped"?
quiz.explain: $in matches if the field equals any listed value.

quiz.q: A collection has documents with and without a color field. What does { color: { $ne: "red" } } return?
options: Only documents with a color that isn't red
Documents with a non-red color and documents with no color
An error, because color is missing in some
quiz.explain: $ne matches any document whose color is not "red", including those where the field is missing.

concepts.name: Sorting, limiting and paging
concepts.summary: Order results with sort, page with limit and skip or a range key, and count with countDocuments.
concepts.why: Lists, feeds and tables all need ordered, paged results that stay fast.
concepts.body:
Cursor methods shape a result: `sort({ createdAt: -1 })` orders it (1 ascending, -1 descending; several keys break ties in order), `limit(n)` caps the count and `skip(n)` jumps ahead. The server always applies them as sort, then skip, then limit, whatever order you chain them in.

Without `sort`, result order is not guaranteed. It often looks like insertion order but can change after updates or when the server picks a different way to run the query, so always sort when order matters, and include a unique field such as `_id` as a final tie-breaker so pages don't overlap.

`skip` paging is easy but gets slower as pages go deeper: to return page 500 the server still walks past every skipped document. For feeds and infinite scroll use **range (keyset) paging**: remember the last value seen and ask for the next ones, e.g. `find({ _id: { $lt: lastId } }).sort({ _id: -1 }).limit(20)`. With an index on the sort key that is fast at any depth.

Counting: `countDocuments(filter)` runs an accurate count of matching documents; `estimatedDocumentCount()` reads a running total the server keeps for the collection, so it is instant but ignores filters. The old `cursor.count()` is outdated; don't use it.

Sorting a large result without a suitable index makes the server sort everything itself, which is slow and limited in size; the indexes lessons show how an index makes sorts cheap.
takeaways: Without sort the order is undefined; add _id as a tie-breaker
sort, skip, limit are applied in that order regardless of chaining
Deep skip is slow; range paging on an indexed key is not
countDocuments for accurate counts, estimatedDocumentCount for a fast total
pitfalls: Relying on natural (insertion) order for pagination without a sort.

quiz.q: You write .limit(5).sort({ price: 1 }). What do you get?
options: An error: sort must come first
quiz.explain: The server sorts first, then applies limit, so you get the 5 cheapest.

concepts.name: Updating documents
concepts.summary: Change documents with updateOne and updateMany using $set, $inc, $unset and $push, and upsert when missing.
concepts.why: Changing a document with operators is atomic, so two users updating it at once can't overwrite each other's changes.
concepts.body:
`updateOne(filter, update, options)` changes the first matching document; `updateMany` changes all matches. The update uses **update operators**, special `$` keys that say how to change the document:

- `$set: { status: "shipped" }` sets fields (creating them, including nested paths), `$unset: { coupon: "" }` removes them,
- `$inc: { stock: -1 }` adds to a number, `$min`/`$max` keep the smaller/larger value,
- `$push: { tags: "sale" }` appends to an array, `$addToSet` appends only if absent, `$pull` removes matching elements,
- `$currentDate: { updatedAt: true }` sets a field to the server's current time.

The result reports `matchedCount` and `modifiedCount`; setting a field to the value it already has counts as matched but not modified.

With `{ upsert: true }` you get an **upsert** (update, or insert if missing): if nothing matches, a new document is built from the equality fields of the filter plus the update. That is handy for counters and "create or update" features.

Each update to one document is atomic, so `$inc` from many clients at once never loses an increment, unlike reading a value, adding in your code and writing it back.

To swap the whole document use `replaceOne(filter, newDoc)`. Passing a plain document without operators to `updateOne` is an error, which protects you from accidentally wiping fields. `findOneAndUpdate` returns the document before or after the change (`returnDocument: "after"`).
takeaways: Use operators: $set/$unset, $inc, $push/$addToSet/$pull
updateOne changes the first match, updateMany all matches
upsert: true inserts when nothing matches
Operator updates are atomic per document: no lost increments
pitfalls: Reading a value, changing it in your own code and writing it back: two users doing this at the same moment overwrite each other; use $inc, or $set with a condition.

quiz.q: Two clients run updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $inc: { n: 1 } }) at the same moment on n = 5. What is n afterwards?
quiz.explain: Each operator update is atomic on the document, so both increments apply.

quiz.q: What does updateOne({ sku: "X" }, { $set: { qty: 1 } }, { upsert: true }) do if no document has sku X?
options: Inserts { sku: "X", qty: 1 } with a new _id
quiz.explain: An upsert builds the new document from the filter's equality fields plus the update.

concepts.name: Deleting documents and collections
concepts.summary: Remove documents with deleteOne and deleteMany, and drop whole collections when appropriate.
concepts.why: Deleting precisely, and knowing which operation keeps indexes, avoids nasty data-loss surprises.
concepts.body:
`deleteOne(filter)` removes the first matching document; `deleteMany(filter)` removes all matches. Both return `deletedCount`. The filter language is the same as for `find`, so the safest habit is to run the `find` first, check what comes back, then switch the method name.

`deleteMany({})` removes every document but keeps the collection, its indexes and its other settings. `db.coll.drop()` removes the collection itself along with its indexes; it is much faster for emptying huge collections, but you have to recreate indexes afterwards.

`findOneAndDelete(filter, { sort })` deletes one document and returns it, all in one step. That makes it the classic way to take the next job from a simple **queue** (a waiting line of jobs, handled first come, first served) without two programs grabbing the same one.

Some data should disappear on its own, such as login records or one-time codes. You don't have to write a clean-up program: create a **TTL index** (TTL means "time to live"): `createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 })`. The server itself deletes documents whose date is older than the limit. It checks about once a minute, so expiry is not to the second.

Many applications prefer **soft deletes**: instead of removing a document they mark it, `$set: { deletedAt: new Date() }`, so it can be restored or checked later. Remember to leave those documents out of your queries.
takeaways: deleteOne / deleteMany take the same filters as find
deleteMany({}) empties but keeps indexes; drop() removes everything
TTL indexes expire documents automatically (about every 60 s)
pitfalls: Running deleteMany with an empty or wrong filter: preview it with find first.

quiz.q: You need to empty a 200-million-document collection but keep using it with the same indexes. What is the trade-off of drop()?
options: drop() also removes the indexes, which you must recreate
drop() only works on empty collections
quiz.explain: drop() is fast but deletes the collection's indexes and options too.

concepts.name: Querying and updating arrays
concepts.summary: Match array elements with plain equality, $all, $size and $elemMatch, and update elements with positional operators.
concepts.why: Arrays are everywhere in document models, and their matching rules surprise most newcomers.
concepts.body:
When a field is an array, a plain filter matches if **any element** matches: `{ tags: "sale" }` finds documents whose `tags` array contains "sale". A filter value that is an array, `{ tags: ["a", "b"] }`, requires the exact array in that order. Use `$all: ["a", "b"]` for "contains both, any order" and `$size: 2` for an exact length.

Arrays of subdocuments need care. `{ "items.sku": "PEN", "items.qty": { $gt: 5 } }` can be satisfied by **different elements**: one item is PEN, another has qty 9. To require one element that satisfies all conditions, use `$elemMatch`: `{ items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "PEN", qty: { $gt: 5 } } } }`.

Updating elements in place:

- `$` (positional) updates the first element matched by the filter: `{ $set: { "items.$.qty": 0 } }`,
- `$[]` updates every element: `{ $inc: { "items.$[].qty": 1 } }`,
- `$[name]` with `arrayFilters` updates only elements matching a condition.

`$push` accepts modifiers: `{ $push: { scores: { $each: [7, 9], $sort: -1, $slice: 3 } } }` appends, sorts and keeps the top three, a neat way to keep a list with a maximum length.

Arrays that grow forever (every comment ever written, every event ever recorded) are a known design mistake: the document keeps getting bigger, slower to read and write, and closer to the 16 MB limit.
takeaways: { arr: x } matches if any element equals x
Use $elemMatch when several conditions must hold on the same element
$ updates the first matched element, $[] all, $[id] those matching arrayFilters
Avoid arrays that grow without bound
pitfalls: Combining conditions on "items.a" and "items.b" and expecting them to apply to the same element.

quiz.q: Which filter finds documents where tags contains both "red" and "big", in any order?
quiz.explain: $all requires every listed value to be present, in any order; the plain array form needs an exact match.

concepts.name: Indexes and explain
concepts.summary: Create single-field, unique and multikey indexes and use explain to see whether a query scans the collection.
concepts.why: Without the right index, a query that is instant on small test data has to read every document once real data piles up.
concepts.body:
Without an index MongoDB answers a query with a **collection scan** (shown as COLLSCAN): it reads every document. An **index** keeps the values of one field in sorted order, each pointing to its document, so finding a value, finding a range of values or sorting by that field takes only a few steps (an index scan, IXSCAN).

MongoDB stores that sorted list as a **B-tree**, a tree shape that stays shallow even with millions of entries, so any value is reached in a handful of hops.

Every collection has a unique index on `_id`. Create others with `createIndex({ email: 1 })`; the 1 or -1 is the sort direction, which only matters for multi-field indexes. Options include:

- `unique: true` to reject duplicates (inserts fail with error 11000),
- `partialFilterExpression` to index only some documents, such as `{ deletedAt: null }`,
- `expireAfterSeconds` to delete documents automatically once a date field is older than a limit (a TTL index), and `sparse` to leave out documents that don't have the field.

Indexing an array field creates a **multikey** index with one entry per element, so `{ tags: "sale" }` is fast too.

Check what a query does with `explain("executionStats")`. Compare `nReturned` with `totalDocsExamined` and `totalKeysExamined`: a good plan examines about as many keys as it returns. Seeing `COLLSCAN` on a query you run often, or examined counts far larger than returned, means you need a better index.

Indexes aren't free: each one takes **RAM** (the server's fast working memory) and disk space, and adds work to every insert and update. Index for the queries you actually run, and drop unused ones (`$indexStats` shows usage).
concepts.code:
for (let i = 0; i < 50000; i++) db.users.insertOne({ email: `u${i}@x.io`, age: i % 90 })

let s = db.users.find({ email: "u4242@x.io" }).explain("executionStats")
s.queryPlanner.winningPlan.stage           // 'COLLSCAN'
s.executionStats.totalDocsExamined         // 50000

db.users.createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true })   // 'email_1'
s = db.users.find({ email: "u4242@x.io" }).explain("executionStats")
s.executionStats.totalKeysExamined         // 1
s.executionStats.totalDocsExamined         // 1   (plan uses IXSCAN)

db.users.insertOne({ email: "u1@x.io" })   // E11000 duplicate key error
db.users.getIndexes().map(i => i.name)     // [ '_id_', 'email_1' ]
takeaways: No index means COLLSCAN: every document is read
explain("executionStats"): compare keys/docs examined with nReturned
unique, partial and TTL are index options; array fields get multikey indexes
Every index slows writes and uses memory: index for real queries
pitfalls: Creating an index for every field just in case: writes get slower and memory fills up.

quiz.q: A query returns 10 documents but explain shows totalDocsExamined: 2000000. What does that suggest?
options: The query lacks a suitable index for its filter
The collection needs to be dropped
quiz.explain: Examining far more documents than returned means the filter is not served by a good index.

concepts.name: Compound indexes and the ESR rule
concepts.summary: Design multi-field indexes in Equality, Sort, Range order so one index serves filter and sort.
concepts.why: Most real queries filter on several fields and sort, and the order of fields in an index decides whether it helps.
concepts.body:
A **compound index** such as `{ status: 1, createdAt: -1 }` is sorted by status first and, within each status, by createdAt. Like a phone book sorted by last then first name, it supports queries on any **prefix**: `{ status }` alone or `{ status, createdAt }`, but not `{ createdAt }` alone.

Order fields with the **ESR rule**:

- **E**quality fields first (`status: "paid"`, `userId: 42`),
- then **S**ort fields (`createdAt: -1`),
- then **R**ange fields (`total: { $gt: 100 }`, `$in` with many values behaves like a range for sorting).

With equality fields first, all matching entries sit next to each other and are already in sort order, so MongoDB doesn't have to sort them itself in RAM (an extra SORT stage in explain). Putting a range field before the sort field breaks that ordering.

Direction matters only between fields: `{ a: 1, b: -1 }` can serve sort `{ a: 1, b: -1 }` or its reverse `{ a: -1, b: 1 }`, but not `{ a: 1, b: 1 }`.

A query is **covered** when the filter and projection use only indexed fields (and exclude `_id` unless it's indexed): the answer comes straight from the index without fetching documents, shown as no FETCH stage in explain.

One well-designed compound index often replaces several single-field ones, because its prefixes serve those queries too.
takeaways: Compound indexes serve queries on a prefix of their fields
Order fields Equality, Sort, Range
Direction matters only relative to other fields in the index
Covered queries are answered from the index alone
pitfalls: Putting the range field before the sort field, which forces MongoDB to sort the results itself.

quiz.q: Query: find({ userId: 7, score: { $gt: 50 } }).sort({ date: -1 }). Which index follows ESR?
quiz.explain: Equality (userId), then sort (date), then range (score).

concepts.name: The aggregation pipeline
concepts.summary: Transform and summarise data with pipeline stages like $match, $group, $project, $sort and $limit.
concepts.why: Reports, dashboards and any server-side data reshaping use aggregation instead of shipping documents to the app.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you want more than matching documents: totals per region, averages per month, a reshaped report. `aggregate([stage, stage, ...])` passes documents through an **aggregation pipeline**: a series of steps, called **stages**, each taking the previous one's output, like an assembly line or chained array methods such as `filter` then `map`.

- `$match` filters (the same filters as `find`); put it first so it can use indexes,
- `$group` groups by `_id` and computes **accumulators**, calculations that boil many values down to one: `$sum`, `$avg`, `$min`, `$max`, `$count`, `$push`, `$addToSet`, `$first`,
- `$project` or `$set` reshape documents and compute fields with expressions such as `$multiply`, `$concat`, `$dateToString`, `$cond`,
- `$sort`, `$limit`, `$skip`, `$count`, `$unwind` and `$lookup` (next lessons).

Inside expressions, `"$field"` (a string starting with `$`) means "the value of this field", while other strings are just text. Grouping by `null` produces a single total over all documents.

MongoDB reorders and merges stages where that's safe, for example moving a `$match` before a `$project`, but write pipelines in the efficient order anyway: filter early, drop big fields early, and sort on indexed fields before grouping when possible.

Each stage may use up to 100 MB of **RAM** (the server's fast working memory). Bigger sorts and groups write temporary data to disk instead, which is allowed by default since MongoDB 6.0. `$out` and `$merge` save the results into a collection, so a summary can be read later instead of recomputed.
takeaways: A pipeline is an array of stages; output of one is input to the next
"$field" references a value; $group needs an _id
$match early so indexes can be used
Stages have a 100 MB memory limit and spill to disk when allowed
pitfalls: Writing "qty" instead of "$qty" in an expression: you get the plain text "qty", not the field's value.

quiz.q: In { $group: { _id: "$category", n: { $sum: 1 } } }, what is n?
options: The sum of a field named 1
The number of documents per category
quiz.explain: $sum: 1 adds 1 for each document in the group, i.e. counts them.

concepts.name: Embedding vs referencing
concepts.summary: Model data around access patterns: embed what is read together and reference what is large, shared or unbounded.
concepts.why: Schema design is the single biggest factor in MongoDB performance and simplicity.
concepts.body:
The guiding rule is **data that is accessed together should be stored together**. Design from the ways your app reads and writes data (its **access patterns**), not from an ER diagram.

**Embed** child data (store it inside the parent document) when it is read with the parent, belongs to one parent and is bounded in size: addresses in a user, line items in an order, the last few reviews on a product. One read fetches everything and a single-document write updates it atomically.

**Reference** (store the other document's `_id` and look it up separately) when:

- the related data is large or grows without bound (all of a user's events),
- it is shared by many parents and updated independently (an author shown on many books),
- it is often queried on its own.

For one-to-many, you can reference from the child (`order.customerId`) or keep an array of ids in the parent when it's small. Many-to-many is usually arrays of ids on one or both sides.

Duplication is acceptable when it saves reads: storing the product name in each order line freezes it at purchase time, which is actually correct. The cost is updating copies when they must change.

Common patterns have names: **subset** (embed the 10 newest reviews, keep the rest in their own collection), **extended reference** (copy a few fields of the referenced document), **bucket** (group readings taken over time, such as one document per sensor per hour), **computed** (store running totals).
takeaways: Model for access patterns: what is read together lives together
Embed bounded, owned data; reference large, shared or unbounded data
Controlled duplication trades write effort for fewer reads
Know the named patterns: subset, extended reference, bucket, computed
pitfalls: Porting a normalized relational schema one table per collection and then combining them again in every query.
Embedding an array that grows forever, like every chat message in a room document.

quiz.q: A blog post has thousands of comments, but the post page shows only the latest 5. Which design fits best?
options: Embed all comments in the post
Put all posts and comments in one document
Store each comment as its own database
Store comments separately and also embed the latest 5 in the post
quiz.explain: The subset pattern keeps the hot data embedded and the unbounded remainder in its own collection.

concepts.name: Using MongoDB from Node.js
concepts.summary: Connect with the official Node.js driver, run CRUD with async/await and reuse one MongoClient.
concepts.why: Applications talk to MongoDB through a driver, and mishandling connections is a classic bug in real apps.
concepts.body:
Install the driver with `npm install mongodb`. npm is Node.js's tool for downloading code other people have published, each bundle being a **package**.

A `MongoClient` keeps a set of open connections to the server ready for reuse, called a **connection pool**, because opening a connection is slow. Create one client when your program starts and use it everywhere. Creating a new client every time your server handles a user's action uses up connections and adds delay.

`client.db("shop").collection("orders")` gives you a collection object with the same methods as the shell: `insertOne`, `find`, `updateMany`, `aggregate`, `createIndex`... Every operation returns a Promise, so use `await`. `find` returns a cursor: call `.toArray()` for small results, or go through large ones one document at a time with `for await (const doc of cursor)`.

Differences from mongosh worth knowing:

- bring the driver's names into your file with `import { MongoClient, ObjectId } from "mongodb"` (an **import** pulls in code from an installed package), and convert string ids with `new ObjectId(id)` before querying `_id`,
- numbers in JavaScript are floating-point; use `Long` or `Decimal128` when you need exact integers beyond 2^53 or money,
- results of `insertOne` and friends are plain objects like `{ acknowledged, insertedId }`.

Your connection string contains your username and password (your **credentials**), so keep it out of your code. Read it from an **environment variable**, a named setting handed to the program when it starts, such as `MONGODB_URI`. Call `client.close()` when the program shuts down.

With TypeScript (a version of JavaScript that checks types before the code runs), `db.collection<Order>("orders")` describes the shape of the documents. Add-ons such as Mongoose build on the driver to add fixed document shapes and checks on values.
takeaways: One MongoClient per program: it is a connection pool
Every operation returns a Promise; cursors support for await
Convert string ids with new ObjectId(id) before matching _id
Keep the connection string in an environment variable
pitfalls: Creating a new MongoClient every time the server handles a user's action instead of reusing one.

quiz.q: A user id arrives in a URL as a 24-character hex string. Why does findOne({ _id: id }) return null?
options: _id is stored as an ObjectId, and a string never equals an ObjectId
The id needs to be lowercased
quiz.explain: BSON comparisons are typed; wrap it with new ObjectId(id).

concepts.name: $lookup joins and $unwind
concepts.summary: Join collections with $lookup and flatten arrays into one document per element with $unwind.
concepts.why: Referenced data has to be combined somewhere, and doing it in the pipeline saves the app from running one extra query per document (the N+1 query problem).
concepts.body:
In SQL you combine rows from two tables with a join. `$lookup` is MongoDB's version: for each input document it finds matching documents in another collection of the same database and puts them in an **array** field. It behaves like a left outer join: input documents with no match are kept, with an empty array.

The simple form matches one field to another: `{ $lookup: { from: "customers", localField: "customerId", foreignField: "_id", as: "customer" } }`. The pipeline form adds `let` variables and a sub-`pipeline` for richer conditions, filtering or projecting the joined documents. Since MongoDB 5.0 you can combine `localField`/`foreignField` with a `pipeline`.

Because the result is always an array (empty when nothing matches), you usually follow with `$unwind` or take the first element with `$first`. `$unwind: "$items"` emits one document per array element; documents with an empty or missing array are dropped unless you pass `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true`.

`$unwind` then `$group` is the standard way to aggregate over array elements, such as revenue per SKU across all orders' line items.

Performance: every input document causes its own lookup, so index the `foreignField` (`_id` already is). Filter with `$match` before `$lookup` to join fewer documents. If a page needs `$lookup` every time it loads, consider embedding or copying part of the data instead.
takeaways: $lookup is a left outer join that yields an array field
$unwind emits one document per array element
$unwind + $group aggregates across array elements
Index foreignField and $match before joining
pitfalls: $unwind silently dropping documents with empty arrays; use preserveNullAndEmptyArrays when you need them.

quiz.q: An order has items: [] and the pipeline runs { $unwind: "$items" }. What happens to that order?
options: It is output once with items: null
It is dropped from the output
It is output once with items: []
quiz.explain: By default $unwind drops documents whose array is empty or missing.

concepts.name: Schema validation
concepts.summary: Enforce required fields, types and value ranges on a collection with $jsonSchema validators.
concepts.why: A flexible schema still needs guard rails so bad writes from any program can't corrupt the data.
concepts.body:
MongoDB can check every inserted and updated document against rules (**validation**), using a **validator** attached to the collection. The usual form is `$jsonSchema`, based on **JSON Schema**, a standard way to describe what valid JSON looks like: required fields, types and ranges. MongoDB's version uses `bsonType` for its own types: `"string"`, `"int"`, `"long"`, `"double"`, `"decimal"`, `"date"`, `"objectId"`, `"array"`, `"object"`.

Set it at creation with `db.createCollection(name, { validator })` or later with the `collMod` command. Two settings control strictness:

- `validationLevel`: `"strict"` (default) checks every insert and update; `"moderate"` skips updates to documents that were already invalid, useful when adding rules to existing data,
- `validationAction`: `"error"` (default) rejects the write; `"warn"` allows it and writes a warning to the server's log (its running record of events).

A rejected write fails with "Document failed validation" and, in recent versions, `errInfo` details explaining which rule failed.

Validation adds to, rather than replaces, the checks in your application: it protects the data from every program that writes to it, including quick one-off programs and other apps. Keep rules to things that must always be true (required keys, types, lists of allowed values, ranges) and leave room to grow, typically by leaving `additionalProperties` unset so new fields can be added. To change the shape over time, a common approach is a `schemaVersion` field plus code that handles both versions while documents are moved to the new shape one by one, whenever they are next written.
takeaways: $jsonSchema validators check inserts and updates on the server
Use bsonType for MongoDB types such as date, int, objectId
validationLevel moderate and validationAction warn help roll rules out gradually
pitfalls: Declaring age as bsonType "int" while the client sends doubles (JavaScript numbers like 30.5): writes fail.

quiz.q: You add a validator to a collection with old invalid documents and want new writes checked, but updates to old invalid docs allowed. Which setting?
quiz.explain: moderate applies rules to inserts and to updates of documents that already satisfy the validator.

concepts.name: Replica sets, read and write concern
concepts.summary: Learn how a replica set keeps copies of your data, picks a new primary when one fails, and how write and read concerns trade safety for speed.
concepts.why: Live MongoDB databases almost always run as a replica set, and how safe your writes are depends on the concerns you choose.
concepts.body:
A single server is a single point of failure: if it dies, your app stops. A **replica set** is a group of `mongod` servers (mongod is the MongoDB server program) that hold the same data, typically three. One is the **primary** and accepts all writes; the others, the **secondaries**, keep copying its changes.

They copy from the **oplog** (operations log), a fixed-size collection where the primary records every change. Each entry is written so that applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once (it is **idempotent**), so a secondary can safely replay entries after a hiccup.

If the primary becomes unreachable, the members hold an **election** and a secondary with the latest data becomes primary, usually within about ten seconds. This automatic switch is a **failover**. Drivers notice the new primary and send writes to it, and retryable writes (on by default) **retry**, that is, try once more, after a failover.

**Write concern** says when a write counts as done: `w: 1` after the primary applies it, `w: "majority"` after a majority of voting members have it (the default since 5.0). Only majority-acknowledged writes are guaranteed to survive a failover; a `w: 1` write can be **rolled back** if the old primary dies before passing it on. `j: true` also waits until the write is in the **journal**, the server's on-disk log of recent changes.

**Read preference** chooses which member serves reads: `primary` (default), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary`, `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest`. Secondaries can lag behind, so reads from them may return **stale data**: data that has since changed.

**Read concern** says what data a read may return: `"local"` (default, may later be rolled back), `"majority"` (only data a majority already has), `"snapshot"` in transactions. To read your own writes back from a secondary, combine majority reads and writes with a causally consistent **session** (a context the driver opens to tie your operations together): each read then waits until it can see your earlier writes.
takeaways: One primary takes writes; secondaries replicate via the oplog
Elections pick a new primary automatically on failure
w: "majority" (default) writes survive failover; w: 1 writes can roll back
Read preference picks the member; read concern picks the durability of data read
pitfalls: Reading from secondaries right after a write and showing users stale data.
Running two data-bearing members only: losing one leaves no majority to elect a primary.

quiz.q: Why can a write acknowledged with w: 1 disappear?
options: The primary may fail before secondaries copy it, and the write is rolled back
It cannot; w: 1 is fully durable
quiz.explain: Only majority-committed writes are guaranteed to survive a failover.

concepts.name: Multi-document transactions
concepts.summary: Change several documents and collections all-or-nothing with ACID transactions, run inside a session with withTransaction.
concepts.why: Some invariants, like moving money between accounts, span several documents and need all-or-nothing writes.
concepts.body:
Single-document writes are always atomic, and good modeling makes them sufficient most of the time. When an operation must change several documents or collections together, MongoDB offers **multi-document ACID transactions** on replica sets and on sharded clusters (data split over several replica sets; see the sharding lesson), but not on a single standalone server.

Transactions run inside a **session**, the driver context you met with replica sets. The easy way is `session.withTransaction(async () => {...})`: you pass the `session` to every operation inside, and the driver commits at the end, aborts on error, and retries the whole function on temporary errors such as write conflicts. If it can't tell whether the commit succeeded, it retries the commit too.

Semantics to know:

- reads inside see a consistent **snapshot**, the data as it was when the transaction started; writes are invisible to others until commit,
- if two transactions modify the same document, the second gets a **WriteConflict** and is retried,
- a transaction should be short: the default limit is 60 seconds (`transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`), and long ones make the server hold on to old versions of data, using up memory,
- use `writeConcern: "majority"` on the transaction for durable commits.

Transactions cost more than single-document writes, so don't wrap every operation in one. Reach for them for real cross-document invariants: transfers, inventory reservation together with order creation, or keeping two collections in sync.
takeaways: Transactions need a replica set or sharded cluster
Pass the session to every operation inside the transaction
withTransaction commits, aborts and retries transient errors for you
Keep them short; prefer single-document atomicity when the model allows
pitfalls: Forgetting { session } on one operation, which then runs outside the transaction and is not rolled back.

quiz.q: Inside withTransaction one update omits the session option and the transaction later aborts. What happens to that update?
options: It stays applied, because it ran outside the transaction
The driver throws before running it
It is retried after the abort
quiz.explain: Only operations given the session are part of the transaction.

concepts.name: Sharding and shard keys
concepts.summary: Split a collection across several replica sets (shards), and choose a shard key that spreads the load and sends each query to few shards.
concepts.why: When one replica set can't hold the data or keep up with writes, the shard key decides whether adding machines helps or one machine gets swamped.
concepts.body:
Every member of a replica set holds all the data, so a replica set can't grow past what one machine can store and write. **Sharding** splits a collection across several replica sets instead: each one is a **shard** and holds part of the data. Together they form a **sharded cluster**.

Applications don't connect to the shards directly. They connect to **mongos**, a program that forwards each operation to the shard holding the data. It knows where data lives from a map kept on the **config servers** (a small replica set of their own).

Data is divided by the **shard key**, one or more indexed fields present in every document. The possible key values are cut into ranges (historically called chunks), and the **balancer**, which runs on the config servers, moves ranges between shards to keep them even.

- **Ranged** sharding keeps nearby key values together, which is good for range queries. But a key that only ever grows, like a timestamp or an ObjectId, sends every insert to the last range: one swamped hot shard.
- **Hashed** sharding places each document by a **hash** of its key (a scrambled number computed from the value). Inserts spread evenly, but a range query on the key must ask every shard.

A good key has many distinct values (high cardinality), no single value that dominates, doesn't just keep growing, and appears in most queries. Queries that include the key are **targeted** to one or a few shards. Queries without it go to every shard and the answers are combined (**scatter-gather**), so they are as slow as the slowest shard.

Compound keys such as `{ tenantId: 1, orderId: 1 }` are common in **multi-tenant** apps, where one system serves many customer companies (tenants): queries per tenant are targeted, while one big tenant can still spread across ranges. You can refine a key by adding fields at the end, or change it entirely with `reshardCollection` (5.0+), which copies all the data, so choose carefully up front.
takeaways: mongos forwards operations, config servers keep the map, shards store the data
The shard key determines distribution and query targeting
Ever-growing ranged keys pile every insert onto one shard; hashed keys spread writes
Queries without the shard key fan out to all shards
pitfalls: Sharding on a field with few distinct values, such as country or status: ranges can't be split and one shard fills up.

quiz.q: A collection is range-sharded on { createdAt: 1 } and receives heavy inserts. What problem appears?
options: All new inserts go to the shard owning the highest range, creating a hot spot
quiz.explain: A key that only ever grows always lands in the top range, so one shard takes every insert.

concepts.name: WiredTiger storage engine
concepts.summary: How MongoDB's storage engine caches, compresses, journals and saves data, and why the working set has to fit in RAM.
concepts.why: Sizing servers and finding the cause of slowdowns require knowing what the storage engine does with memory and disk.
concepts.body:
Every database has a part that actually writes data to disk and reads it back: its **storage engine**. MongoDB's is **WiredTiger**. Each collection and each index is a separate B-tree file on disk.

**Cache.** Reading from disk is slow, so WiredTiger keeps recently used data, uncompressed, in its own **cache** in RAM. By default the cache gets half of (RAM minus 1 GB), and at least 256 MB; a GB (**gigabyte**) is about a thousand MB.

The rest of RAM isn't wasted: the **operating system** (Linux, say) keeps recently read parts of files there too, still compressed. Data moves between disk and cache in pages, small blocks of a B-tree.

Performance is best when the **working set**, the documents and index pages you touch regularly, fits in the cache. When it doesn't, reads keep going to disk and WiredTiger must keep pushing old pages out (**eviction**). That runs on background **threads**, separate lines of work inside the server; under heavy pressure the threads serving your queries are drafted in to help, and queries slow down sharply.

**Compression.** Collections use snappy compression by default (zstd and zlib are options). Indexes use prefix compression, which stores the shared start of neighbouring keys only once. Disk usage is usually much smaller than the data itself.

**Concurrency.** Many operations can work on one collection at the same time (that is concurrency). WiredTiger keeps several versions of a document while it changes (**MVCC**): readers see a **snapshot**, the data as of one moment, and when two writers change the same document one of them retries, instead of locking the whole collection.

**Durability.** Each write goes into memory and into the **journal**, a **write-ahead log**: a file where changes are recorded before they reach the data files. It is saved to disk every 100 ms by default, or at once with `j: true`. Every 60 seconds a **checkpoint** writes a consistent copy of all data files. After a crash, MongoDB starts from the last checkpoint and replays the journal.

Watch `db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache` for bytes in cache versus the maximum, and for the share of changed data not yet written to disk.
concepts.code:
const c = db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache
c["maximum bytes configured"]          // e.g. 7.5 GiB on a 16 GiB machine
c["bytes currently in the cache"]
c["tracked dirty bytes in the cache"]
c["pages read into cache"]             // climbing fast = working set > cache

const s = db.orders.stats()
s.size                                 // logical, uncompressed data bytes
s.storageSize                          // on-disk bytes after compression
s.totalIndexSize
takeaways: Default cache = 50% of (RAM - 1 GB); keep the working set in it
Snappy compression for data, prefix compression for indexes
Document-level concurrency with MVCC snapshots
Journal + 60-second checkpoints give crash recovery
pitfalls: Sizing servers by data size alone: what must fit in RAM is the working set, especially indexes.

quiz.q: After a crash, how does WiredTiger recover?
options: It rebuilds every index from scratch
It starts from the last checkpoint and replays the journal
It copies data from the oplog of a secondary only
It cannot; data since the last backup is lost
quiz.explain: Checkpoints give a consistent base and the journal replays writes made since.

concepts.name: Query planner and plan cache
concepts.summary: See how MongoDB picks among possible plans, remembers the winner in its plan cache, and how to diagnose and steer that choice.
concepts.why: Sudden slowdowns often come from MongoDB switching a query to a worse plan (a plan flip), and fixing them requires reading the planner's decisions.
concepts.body:
When several indexes could serve a query, MongoDB can't know in advance which is fastest, so it tries them. The query planner builds **candidate plans** and races them in a short trial: each runs until one returns a batch of results (101 documents by default) or has done enough work. The most productive plan wins.

The winner is stored in the **plan cache**, keyed by the **query shape**: the structure of the filter, sort and projection, ignoring the actual values. Later queries with the same shape reuse it.

Entries in the plan cache are removed when the indexes change, on restart, or when the stored plan performs much worse than when it was first chosen, which starts a new race. This is why the same query can be fast for one value and slow for another: a plan chosen for a **selective** value (one that matches few documents) is reused for a value that matches millions.

Diagnosing:

- `explain("allPlansExecution")` shows every candidate, its trial statistics, and the `rejectedPlans`,
- `db.coll.getPlanCache().list()` shows cached plans; `.clear()` resets them,
- the slow query log and the **profiler**, a MongoDB feature that records slow operations (`db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 })`), show `planSummary`, `keysExamined` and `docsExamined`.

Steering: `hint({ field: 1 })` forces an index for one query; **index filters** (`planCacheSetFilter`) limit the choices for a shape. The better fix is usually an index that clearly beats the others (ESR), or removing redundant indexes that confuse the race. Modern versions run many queries in the slot-based execution engine (SBE), a newer and faster way of executing plans, visible in explain as `queryPlanner.winningPlan.slotBasedPlan`.
takeaways: Candidate plans race in a trial; the winner is cached per query shape
A cached plan may be poor for different constants: plan flips
allPlansExecution, the plan cache and the profiler reveal decisions
Prefer a dominating index over hints
pitfalls: Sprinkling hint() in application code: it keeps forcing a plan even after data or indexes change.

quiz.q: What is the plan cache keyed by?
options: The query shape: structure of filter, sort and projection
quiz.explain: Plans are cached per shape so queries differing only in values reuse a plan.
